section_title: Why do character and the ability to teach belong together?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 2 An overseer, then, must be above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,

context_lines: This verse begins the detailed qualifications for an overseer. Paul places the ability to teach alongside a life marked by faithfulness, self-control, respectability and hospitality.

Above reproach is a character requirement, not merely a title given to someone who wants the role. The following verses extend the picture to gentleness, freedom from greed, household care, maturity and reputation.

The word translated able to teach is didaktikos (dee-dak-tee-KOSS). [Thayer’s lexicon](https://biblehub.com/greek/1317.htm) describes aptitude and skill in teaching. Paul’s concern includes a real ability to help the community understand, alongside a life consistent with that instruction.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand this list as requiring tested character, faithful conduct and the ability to teach. They differ in how the office is related to other church offices.

The Baptist [1689 Confession, 26.8–9](https://www.the1689confession.com/1689/chapter-26), identifies bishops or elders and deacons as the church’s appointed officers. The Catholic [Catechism, paragraph 1554](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_two/section_two/chapter_three/article_6/iii_the_three_degrees_of_the_sacrament_of_holy_orders.index.html), describes bishops, priests and deacons as three degrees of ordained ministry. The shared call to character stands within different accounts of church order.

The marriage phrase also needs careful application. The [BSB footnote](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_timothy/3.htm) offers faithful to his wife. [Wesley’s note on verse 2](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-first-epistle-to-timothy/) reads it as excluding unfaithful marriage practices, rather than requiring every overseer to marry or banning every second marriage. Catholic practice likewise does not require marriage: [Catechism 1579–1580](https://www.vatican.va/content/catechism/en/part_two/section_two/chapter_three/article_6/vi_who_can_receive_this_sacrament.html) describes the Latin Church’s normal celibacy rule and the different Eastern practice of ordaining married men. These examples do not settle every church’s rules about divorce, remarriage or selection.
god_plan_lines: [Acts 20:17, 28–32](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/20.htm) connects the elders’ oversight with care for the church God obtained, protection from harmful teaching and the word of grace that builds His people and gives an inheritance. The qualifications here serve that larger care for a people belonging to Him.

[1 Peter 5:1–4](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_peter/5.htm) places the elders’ service under Christ the Chief Shepherd, with His appearing ahead. Leaders are to be willing examples, rather than ruling for greed or control. Their work prepares and cares for His people in light of that future.
current_position_lines: In [Who Shepherds the Church?](https://thewayofscripture.com/studies/who-shepherds-the-church.html), we emphasize that rejecting a titled hierarchy does not mean rejecting qualified teaching. Those caring for the church must be able to explain Scripture and correct teaching that departs from it. Shared leadership needs people equipped to keep the community’s study anchored in the text.

editorial_review.position_source_detail: Who Shepherds the Church?, lines 82–92, especially direct 1 Timothy 3:2 at line 88: qualified teachers who explain Scripture and correct error; shared leadership is not a leaderless discussion.
